# Project title

**Occupational Mobility Is Not One Thing: Evidence from the Canadian Labour Market**

# Project description, rationale, and objectives

## Background and motivation

Labour markets must continually reallocate workers across occupations in response to technological change, policy, and economic shocks. While entry and exit account for part of this adjustment, a substantial share occurs through **occupational mobility** among existing workers.

A large empirical literature models labour market dynamics using task- and skill-based frameworks, in which occupations are characterized by their underlying skill requirements @autor2013task @acemoglu2011skills. In these models, workers accumulate human capital that is partially transferable across occupations, implying that mobility is more likely between occupations with similar skill profiles @yamaguchi2012task.

Empirical work operationalizes this idea using measures of occupational distance derived from task content or skill similarity @gathmann2010general. These approaches embed occupations in a continuous skill space and implicitly assume that mobility is local within that space.

At the same time, a parallel literature emphasizes the role of institutions and occupational structure in shaping mobility @weeden2002. Credential requirements, licensing, and occupational classifications can constrain entry into certain occupations, independent of skill similarity.

Despite this, most empirical analyses adopt a single notion of distance—typically skill-based—and do not directly evaluate whether it provides an adequate representation of mobility frictions.

## Knowledge gap

Two key gaps emerge from the existing literature.

First, there is limited evidence on **which notion of occupational distance best explains observed mobility patterns**. Standard empirical approaches—such as gravity-style models @anderson_vanwincoop_2003—jointly estimate origin effects, destination effects, and  distance sensitivity. In these models, misspecification of the distance measure can be absorbed by other parameters, making it difficult to assess whether the chosen distance metric accurately captures mobility frictions. As a result, existing estimates do not provide a clean comparison of competing distance measures.

Second, most analyses implicitly assume that mobility operates under a single, homogeneous mechanism across the labour market. However, occupations differ substantially in the extent to which entry is constrained by formal educational pathways or credentials.

Some occupations draw from narrow, well-defined educational pipelines and require specific degrees, certifications, or licensing. Others recruit from diverse educational backgrounds and allow more flexible entry pathways.

This suggests that the relevance of different distance measures may vary systematically across occupations.

In particular:

-   Skill distance may best rationalize occupational mobility where education specificity is low.
-   Binary distance may best rationalize (the lack of) occupational mobility when education is highly specific and occupation is TEER 1. 
-   Hierarchical distance may best rationalize occupational mobility elsewhere.

## Policy relevance

Understanding the structure of occupational mobility is directly relevant to labour market policy.

Many policy interventions—such as training programs, reskilling initiatives, and workforce planning—implicitly assume that workers can transition between occupations based on skill similarity. However, if mobility is constrained by institutional factors such as credentialing requirements or tightly defined educational pathways, these assumptions may not hold.

This distinction has important implications:

-   In occupations with open entry pathways, targeted training and short-cycle reskilling programs may facilitate rapid adjustment
-   In occupations with tight entry pathways, adjustment may depend on longer-term investments in formal education and credentialing systems

Mischaracterizing the nature of mobility frictions may therefore lead to ineffective or misaligned policy responses.

By identifying which notion of occupational distance best explains observed mobility—and how this varies across the labour market—this project provides evidence to support more effective workforce development and labour market adjustment strategies.

## Objectives

This project addresses these gaps by evaluating competing measures of occupational distance within a unified framework.

The primary research questions are:

1.  Which notion of occupational distance best rationalizes observed occupational mobility in Canada?
2.  Does the explanatory power of different distance measures vary across segments of the labour market?
3.  To what extent does occupational mobility reflect local reallocation versus non-local transitions associated with new credentials?

To address these questions, the project will:

-   Construct transition matrices of occupational mobility using Census 2016-2021 Longitudinal File (CEN_2016_2021)
-   Develop three alternative distance measures:
    -   a skill-based distance derived from O\*NET descriptors
    -   a hierarchical distance based on the NOC classification
    -   a binary distance (zero cost to stay, all moves equally costly)
-   Evaluate how well each distance measure explains observed local mobility (no new highest educational attainment) using an entropy-regularized optimal transport framework
-   Examine heterogeneity in local mobility by segmenting the labour market according to the concentration of educational pathways into occupations
-   For non-local mobility (new highest educational attainment), regress distance traveled on Education and Destination specificity (plus origin fixed effects). i.e.  We hypothesize that the more specific the education (in terms of associated occupations) and the more specific the occupation (in terms of associated educational background) the larger the distance traveled will be between 2016 and 2021 occupations. 

# Data requirements

## Justification for using microdata

The analysis requires individual-level transitions between occupations over time, which cannot be obtained from:

-   Public Use Microdata Files (PUMFs)
-   Custom tabulations
-   Remote access systems

The project relies on Census 2016-2021 Longitudinal File (CEN_2016_2021), which allow observation of individuals’ occupations at two points in time. This is essential to construct the origin–destination transition matrix and analyze mobility patterns.

## Dataset(s) required 

- Census 2016-2021 Longitudinal File (CEN_2016_2021)  

- Access to all linked records, including those with missing values for the variables of interest are required.

### Sample description (Updated)

-   Unit of analysis: individual workers
-   We create a  *measurement complete* subset of the linked data where occupation, field of study, highest educational attainment, class of worker, and **age** are all observed in both 2016 and 2021.
- All modelling is conducted on the measurement complete subset, but we also need to query the missingness (relative to all linked observations) in order to quantify potential selection bias. 

- For example, the non-local partition is restricted to individuals who acquire a new highest educational attainment between 2016 and 2021 and report an occupation in both periods. Thus the excluded population is disproportionately those whose human capital increased the most. The most demanding programs --- medicine, law, dentistry --- require sufficiently intensive study that concurrent employment is largely precluded, meaning students in these programs are less likely to report a 2016 occupation and thus are excluded from the sample. The most demanding programs tend also to be the most specific, and the human capital increment they confer is large --- generating the longest new-attainment-driven occupational jumps. Excluding these observations truncates the upper tail of the distance distribution precisely where education specificity is highest. Estimates of the relationship between education specificity and distance traveled should accordingly be interpreted as lower bounds on the true relationship in the full population of new educational attainment. A diagnostic plot of each education's occupation specificity against the proportion of workers missing a 2016 occupation --- computed by 2021 education --- will quantify the magnitude of this truncation.

### Geography

-   National

### Variable list (Updated)

Variables expected to be used include:

-   Occupation (ideally as a NOC 2021 code in both periods)
-   Highest level of educational attainment
-   Field of study (CIP)
-   Class of Worker 
-   **Age**

I am requesting Age be included for two purposes:

1) For local mobility, age tertiles replace occupation education 
specificity (OES) tertiles as the sub-regime classifier in a 
placebo partition test. The theoretical prior is that OES --- 
which measures the credential selectivity of the origin occupation 
directly --- should produce more decisive horse race results than 
age, which predicts mobility only as a proxy for accumulated 
specific human capital. If this is borne out, it constitutes 
evidence that OES is capturing the underlying mechanism rather 
than acting as a demographic correlate.

2) For non-local mobility, age is excluded from the main 
specifications on theoretical grounds: in the non-local sample, 
age predicts jump distance primarily through its correlation with 
origin occupation quality --- younger workers acquiring credentials 
tend to hold lower-skill 2016 occupations, generating mechanically 
larger measured jumps. This is not a confound to be removed but 
rather the wormhole mechanism operating as intended. However, a 
referee may reasonably request age controls, and having age 
available allows this robustness check to be conducted in advance.


Derived variables will include:

-   Indicators of occupational transitions between 2016 and 2021, constructed from origin–destination occupation pairs at the individual level
-   Aggregated transition matrices and associated origin and destination marginals, constructed using survey weights
-   Measures of education and occupation specificity, derived from NOC–education distributions (e.g., based on published cross-tabulations)
-   Occupational distance matrices, including both skill-based measures constructed from publicly available O\*NET data and hierarchical measures based on the NOC classification

## Will datasets be merged or pooled together?

No direct merging of microdata files is required.

# Methodology

## Sample size and confidentiality

The Census 2016-2021 Longitudinal File (CEN_2016_2021) provides a large sample size and the number of observations is expected to be sufficient to:

-   Construct reliable transition matrices at detailed occupational levels
-   Support statistically reliable analysis of occupational mobility patterns

All outputs will comply with Statistics Canada confidentiality requirements. Descriptive statistics will be reported at an aggregated level, including sample counts, mobility rates, and summary statistics of occupational transitions and distance measures. All outputs will be disclosure-controlled, with no reporting of small cells or fine-grained transition matrices.

## Modelling

The analysis uses entropy-regularized optimal transport to model occupational mobility.

The method:

-   Takes observed origin and destination totals as given
-   Computes a transition matrix that minimizes mobility costs subject to these constraints
-   Uses a distance matrix to represent the cost of moving between occupations

The optimization problem is solved using a standard numerical procedure (Sinkhorn iteration).

Three alternative distance specifications will be evaluated:

-   A model based on skill similarity
-   A model based on hierarchical proximity within the NOC classification
-   A model based on binary costs, with zero cost for remaining in the same occupation and a constant positive cost for all occupational changes. 

Model performance will be assessed by comparing how well each specification reproduces the observed transition matrix.

The approach does not involve training or tuning a predictive model and does not use machine learning techniques.

## Descriptive statistics

Following SDAC guidelines, the project methodology will focus on modeling, with a minimal focus on descriptive statistics. The amount of descriptive statistics requested for release will be kept to a minimum and will only be released to support the project’s research objectives and provide contextual information (i.e., to describe the sample). Vetting requests for intermediary output will be kept to a minimum, and descriptives will be released near the end of the project in order to minimize residual disclosure issues.

Descriptive statistics will be reported at an aggregated level and will include sample construction and counts (e.g., number of individuals, number of occupational transitions, and shares across local, non-local, and mismeasured partitions), along with high-level mobility rates by education change and broad occupational groupings. The analysis will also report summary statistics of occupational distance measures (e.g., distributions of distances and comparisons across partitions), as well as aggregated transition patterns using coarse occupational groupings. Additional diagnostics will summarize the composition of partitions and the structure of the occupational mapping (e.g., prevalence of one-to-one, many-to-one, and one-to-many mappings). All reported statistics will be sufficiently aggregated to ensure disclosure control and will not include small cell counts or fine-grained transition matrices.

# External Data

The analysis will incorporate publicly available [O\*NET](https://www.onetcenter.org/database.html#individual-files) data to construct measures of occupational similarity. These data provide descriptors of skills, knowledge, abilities, and work activities, which will be mapped to Canadian occupations using established crosswalks.

In addition, the public [Occupation by major field of study (detailed, 4-digit): Canada, provinces and territories](https://www150.statcan.gc.ca/t1/tbl1/en/tv.action?pid=9810040401) table will be used to construct measures of education specificity and destination gating.

No confidential external data will be used. Public data sources are used solely to construct derived measures and will not be linked at the individual level to the microdata.
